summary: Surveys current practices large ISPs use to secure layer 2 and layer 3 infrastructure devices, based on information from people responsible for those networks. It is informational and does not set new rules.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo records how large internet providers protect the routers and switches that run their networks in 2007. It pairs the threats they worry about with the measures they use, from badge-locked rooms and a separate management network to filters that reject forged addresses. It is a survey, so it sets no rules.

questions: how do isps protect routers from attacks
subtitle: How large internet providers protect the routers and switches that run their networks.

tldr.problem: Large internet service providers knew well how to secure their own infrastructure devices, but no written document enumerated the practices they used, and there was no shared reference for what those practices were.
tldr.mechanism: The survey collects practices from the people who run those networks and groups them by the operational function being protected: physical access, device management, the data path, the routing control plane, software and configuration integrity, logging, filtering and denial-of-service tracking.
tldr.outcome: The document records what was deployed in 2007, including its gaps: IPsec was judged too cumbersome to use, syslog had no security at all, and routing updates were never kept confidential. It is informational and sets no rules.

today: RFC 4778 is an Informational document published in January 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a snapshot rather than a specification, so its findings describe the practices large ISPs reported using at that time.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Large internet service providers had long known how to secure their own routers and switches, but no written document collected those practices. RFC 4778 is a survey of the practices in use at the time, built from information gathered from the people who define and implement secure infrastructure in provider networks. It does not specify an Internet standard and sets no new rules.

The scope is limited to practices that reduce the risk to network availability and reliability. Securing customer traffic itself is outside the scope. The survey covers layer 2 and layer 3 infrastructure devices. It is written mainly around IPv4, although many of the same practices also apply to IPv6, and both IPv4 and IPv6 infrastructures are taken into account.

Each section follows the same shape: the operational function, the attacks that apply to it, the practices deployed against them, and the security services those practices deliver. Those services are user authentication, user authorization, data origin authentication, access control, data integrity, data confidentiality, auditing and logging, and denial-of-service mitigation. The RFC stresses that the service matters more than the protocol that provides it.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo collects what big internet providers actually do to protect the gear that runs their networks. It does not set any rules. It only records the practices in use when it was written.

sections.title: Threat Model and Attack Sources
sections.content:
The threat model follows the Internet Security Glossary, RFC 2828. A threat turns into an attack through reconnaissance, man-in-the-middle interception, exploitation of known protocol flaws, message insertion, message diversion or deletion, and message modification. Denial of service is usually a consequence of an attack rather than a category of its own: it can come from too much traffic, from exploiting a protocol, or from inserting, deleting, diverting or modifying messages.

Attacks differ along four lines. They are active when the attacker writes to the network and passive when the attacker only reads it. They are on-path when the attacker sits between two hosts and off-path when the attacker can only send. They are insider attacks when someone already authorised misuses that access, and outside attacks when the attacker is not authorised. And they are deliberate or unintentional, because a configuration error or a software bug can be as devastating to network availability as a deliberate attack.

The consequences fall into four classes: unauthorized disclosure of data, deception in which an authorised party receives false data and believes it, disruption of service, and usurpation in which an unauthorised party takes control of services. The RFC notes that attackers usually combine several attacks. A miscreant may listen first to learn which addresses belong to routers, capture a router password sent in cleartext, compromise the router, and then send bogus routing updates to redirect traffic or capture more.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists the ways networks get attacked: watching traffic, pretending to be somebody else, exploiting a protocol flaw, or injecting and deleting messages. It also says what an attacker is after, such as reading data that should stay private, feeding false information, taking over a service, or shutting it down.

sections.title: Physical Access and Device Management
sections.content:
Devices sit in restrictive places reached with card-key badges, and the badge systems record who entered which location and when. A fail-back master key exists for when the badge system is down, and its use is logged. Console logins are always password protected and time out after a period of inactivity, typically between 3 and 10 minutes. Vendors differ: some require a second authentication step before granting privileged access.

Console access is architected over an out-of-band management network, where control traffic takes a separate path from customer traffic. Management itself uses virtual terminal access such as Telnet or SSH, SNMP, or HTTP. The survey found that HTTP management was never used and was explicitly disabled at every large ISP interviewed. A terminal server sits at each location and operators reach it over SSH. Dial-in access exists as a backup, usually with dial-back, encrypting modems or one-time-password modems.

Authentication and authorization come from AAA servers, with RADIUS or TACACS+ holding a record per user and per privilege level. Static passwords expire after a specified period, usually 30 days. A single local account is kept as a fallback for the highest privilege level, known to very few people, and its password is regenerated every 2 to 3 months and immediately when a holder leaves the company. SSH is always used for terminal access. Where equipment cannot support it, Telnet is allowed only from designated jumphosts, and the AAA logs are then watched more closely. SNMP, when used, is for read queries only, restricted to specific hosts, with community strings changed every 30 to 90 days; SNMP read-write is disabled by configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Critical gear lives in locked rooms with badge readers. Staff reach it through a separate management network using encrypted remote login, and a central list decides who may log in and what each person is allowed to do.

sections.title: The Data Path and Filtering
sections.content:
Attack traffic in the data path can arrive with spoofed source or destination addresses, or with mangled header fields that reset connections, send unwanted ICMP redirects, add unwanted IP options, or fragment packets. Filtering and rate limiting are the main tools for keeping malicious traffic from making the network unavailable. Providers without performance problems follow BCP 38 (RFC 2827) and BCP 84 (RFC 3704) for ingress filtering, and some also block unexpected source and destination addresses so that an exchange peer cannot steal transit with static routes. Layer 4 filtering is widely seen as useful, but it is usually a last option because of the administrative overhead and because ISPs are reluctant to act as the Internet firewall.

Unicast reverse path forwarding is not deployed consistently. In strict mode a packet is rejected unless its source address matches a prefix in the routing table and the incoming interface expects traffic from it; in loose mode any route to the source is enough. Some providers apply it at DS3 link speeds and below, because support above that was inconsistent. At the layer 2 level, MAC address filtering and port security are not used in large deployments, because troubleshooting becomes unmanageable across thousands of switches.

Filtering is split into three areas: data plane filters for transit traffic, management filters for SSH, Telnet, SNMP, NTP, HTTP, DNS, TFTP, FTP, SCP and Syslog, and routing filters for routing information. Services that are not used are turned off. IPv6 needs specific ICMP messages to work, so ICMP cannot be filtered wholesale and granular ICMPv6 filtering is deployed instead. Announcements longer than a /48 for IPv6 and a /24 for IPv4 are filtered out of eBGP for non-customer traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic crossing the network is checked with filters and rate limits, so forged addresses and broken packets are dropped before they can overload the pipes. Some providers also drop any packet whose source address could not have arrived from that side.

sections.title: Securing the Routing Control Plane
sections.content:
The routing control plane carries the traffic that establishes and maintains routing information. It is attacked by eavesdropping, by inserting or modifying messages, and by impersonating a peer. Some ISPs use MD5 authentication to check the sending peer and to show the data was not altered in transit; others deploy it only when a customer asks. Route filters and the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (RFC 3682) add sanity checks: GTSM uses the IPv4 TTL or the IPv6 Hop Limit so only neighbours can reach each other, and is usually deployed only between internal BGP peers because support is inconsistent across vendors and operating system versions.

Access control over routing comes from packet filters, route filters, incoming and outgoing prefix filters for customers and for peers, AS-PATH filters, route dampening, and limits on how many prefixes a peer may send. That limit catches misconfiguration and overload. The RFC warns that automatically re-establishing a session after an idle timeout can keep injecting instability into the routing table, so shutting the session down until an operator clears it is sometimes better. Some large ISPs require routes to be registered in an Internet Routing Registry, and some do not propagate interface IP addresses, which reduces what an attacker can aim at.

Data confidentiality is not implemented for routing, because the concern is the integrity and validity of updates rather than secrecy, and IPsec is judged too complex and time consuming to be operationally viable. The RFC also notes that MD5 deployment has run into software bugs and a lack of graceful re-keying, and that some ISPs fear MD5 would itself make them a better denial-of-service target.
sections.plainLanguage: Route exchanges are protected by checks that a message came from a real neighbour and was not changed on the way, plus filters that refuse routes a peer should not be sending. Nobody encrypts route traffic, because the worry is lies and tampering rather than secrecy.

sections.title: Logging and Denial-of-Service Mitigation
sections.content:
Logging raises three questions: what to record, how long to keep it, and how to protect it in transit and at rest. Most providers log on an exception basis, meaning traffic that was not allowed, so the log servers are not overwhelmed and the logs stay usable. Records hold source and destination addresses, layer 4 port numbers and a timestamp, and they travel to syslog servers over the out-of-band network, because there is virtually no security between the device and the server. Routers also log routing protocol state changes, all device access whether or not it authenticated, all commands issued, all configuration changes, and router events such as boot-ups and flaps. Syslog is unreliable, so some providers place passive devices in the path to watch routing updates as a backup.

Against denial-of-service traffic the RFC lists five techniques. Sinkhole routing injects a more specific route for known attack traffic so that it is redirected to a device where it can be analysed. Black hole triggered routing (RFC 3882) uses BGP to propagate routes that send attack traffic to the null interface, where it is dropped. Unicast reverse path forwarding validates whether the source address is legitimate. Rate limiting caps bandwidth or packets per second for a traffic type; it does not stop an attack but can limit the damage. Some providers also add vendor features that simplify filtering and rate limiting of control traffic, because an attack on control traffic is more damaging to a critical device than an attack on ordinary data.

The RFC notes that some large providers do not concern themselves with attack streams below 1G in bandwidth, and that at the last count the number of hosts making up large distributed denial-of-service botnets exceeded 1 million. Section 3 closes by saying the document only lists practices and does not in itself pose a security risk. The appendix lists protocol-level attacks, including ARP flooding, spoofed IP addresses, the source route, record route and timestamp options, fragmentation, the ToS or DSCP field, the checksum and the TTL field, and the corresponding IPv6 attacks apart from fragmentation and broadcast.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers keep logs of refused traffic and of every command run on a device, sent over the separate management network. When a flood arrives they can steer the attack traffic into a trap, drop it, or limit how much of the pipe it may take.

items.title: User Authentication
items.text: Confirms who is asking for access.

items.title: User Authorization
items.text: Limits what an authenticated user may do.

items.title: Data Origin Authentication
items.text: Checks that traffic really came from the claimed peer.

items.title: Access Control
items.text: Filtering, in practice, to keep unwanted traffic out.

items.title: Data Integrity
items.text: Detects data altered on its way.

items.title: Data Confidentiality
items.text: Keeps data unreadable to anyone else.

items.title: Auditing and Logging
items.text: Records who did what, and when.

items.title: DoS Mitigation
items.text: Limits the damage from floods and other attacks.
